## Safety: the model and its wrapper

The ethics statement admits that R1 can be jailbroken, and that stronger reasoning can make harmful plans more feasible. A public model can also be fine-tuned in ways that remove safety protections.

Appendix D.3 evaluates this in several ways: six public benchmarks, an in-house set of 1,120 questions across a taxonomy of 4 categories and 28 subcategories, 50 languages, and jailbreak prompts. Many deployments add an external **risk control system**: user queries are keyword-matched, flagged dialogues are sent to DeepSeek-V3 with a review prompt, and unsafe ones are retracted.

The numbers matter. On the in-house set, R1 without the risk control system has an unsafe rate of 25.2%; with it, 8.5%, but rejections rise to 27.3%. Under jailbreak prompts, R1 without risk control reaches an unsafe rate of 85.9% (Table 11), versus 4.3% with it. The authors note that open-weights models run locally lack this layer and recommend developers add similar controls. Their overall judgment is a "moderate" intrinsic safety level, comparable to GPT-4o (2024-05-13).
